etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English ticket, from Middle French etiquet m, estiquet m, and etiquette f, estiquette f (“a bill, note, label, ticket”), from Old French estechier, estichier, estequier (“to attach, stick”), (compare Picard estiquier (“to stick, pierce”)), from Frankish *stikkjan, *stekan (“to stick, pierce, sting”), from Proto-Germanic *stikaną, *stikōną, *staikijaną (“to be sharp, pierce, prick”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)teyg- (“to be sharp, to stab”). Doublet of etiquette. More at stick.

definitions.definition: A pass entitling the holder to admission to a show, concert, sporting event, etc.
A pass entitling the holder to board a train, a bus, a plane, or other means of transportation.
A permit to operate a machine on a construction site.
A certificate or token of a share in a lottery or other scheme for distributing money, goods, etc.
A certificate of qualification as a ship's master, pilot, or other crew member.

quote.citation: 1942 July-August, T. F. Cameron, “How the Staff of a Railway is Recruited”, in Railway Magazine, page 207:
quote.text: The variety of the demands of the railways for staff is almost endless. They require men with master's tickets as dock masters and to command their steamships.

definitions.definition: (figurative) A solution to a problem; something that is needed in order to do something.

quote.citation: 1884, Mark Twain, chapter 34, in Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, →ISBN:
quote.text: "Here's the ticket. This hole's big enough for Jim to get through if we wrench off the board."

definitions.definition: A small document that acts as proof of something, often thereby granting the holder some ability.
A citation for a traffic violation.
(usually technical support) A service request, used to track complaints or requests that an issue be handled.

quote.citation: 2022 September 19, HarryBlank, “Beyond Repair”, in SCP Foundation‎[1], archived from the original on 15 September 2024:
quote.text: "Yeah." It was him, alright; if the world's weariest pair of workboots hadn't tipped her off, his world-weary voice certainly would have. "Where were you?""My quarters. We've got a full ticket set today, and techs work best without oversight." Neither of these things was untrue, though the curation was more than a little dishonest."Maybe yours do." Nascimbeni rolled out, back flat against a neon orange creeper, and sat up with an audible wince. "Mine fuck the dog."

definitions.definition: (politics, informal) A list of candidates for an election, or a particular theme to a candidate's manifesto.

quote.citation: 2019 March 3, Simon van Zuylen-Wood, “When Did Everyone Become a Socialist?”, in New York Magazine‎[2]:
quote.text: Candidates like Ocasio-Cortez and Sanders are no longer too precious to run on the Democratic ticket, though the proposals they suggest are so ambitious — like Medicare for All, a Green New Deal, and free public college — that they don’t feel like compromises at all.

quote.citation: 2020 November 7, Chelsea Janes, “Kamala Harris, daughter of Jamaican and Indian immigrants, elected nation’s first female vice president”, in Washington Post‎[3]:
quote.text: Harris’s victory comes 55 years after the Voting Rights Act abolished laws that disenfranchised Black Americans, 36 years after the first woman ran on a presidential ticket and four years after Democrats were devastated by the defeat of Hillary Clinton

quote.citation: a. 1662 (date written), Thomas Fuller, The History of the Worthies of England, London:  […]  J[ohn] G[rismond,] W[illiam] L[eybourne] and W[illiam] G[odbid], published 1662, →OCLC:
quote.text: He constantly read his lectures twice a week for above forty years, giving notice of the time to his auditors in a ticket on the school doors.

definitions.definition: (dated) A tradesman's bill or account (hence the phrase on ticket and eventually on tick).

quote.text: Your courtier is mad to take up silks and velvets / On ticket for his mistress.

definitions.definition: A label affixed to goods to show their price or description.

quote.citation: 1878, Mrs. James Mason, All about Edith, page 124:
quote.text: I asked for a card, please, and she was quite put about, and said that she didn't require tickets to get in where she visited.

quote.citation: 1899, The Leisure Hour: An Illustrated Magazine for Home Reading:
quote.text: "Mr. Gibbs come in just now," said Mrs. Blewett, "and left his ticket over the chimley. There 'tis. I haven't touched it."

quote.citation: 1999, Doug Most, Always in Our Hearts, page 148:
quote.text: […]  I need a ticket, Bobby.” Agnor knew a ticket meant a search warrant.

definitions.definition: To issue someone a ticket, as for travel or for a violation of a local or traffic law.
